nameStory: Three-toothed cinquefoil gets its name from its distinctive leaves, which end in three neat little teeth at the tip. The word 'cinquefoil' comes from French meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the five-leaflet pattern common in this plant family, though our three-toothed friend is a bit of a rebel with its three-part leaf tips.
description: Three-toothed cinquefoil is a low-growing, woody perennial that forms dense mats across rocky terrain. This hardy little plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches, spreading horizontally instead to create thick carpets of leathery leaves. In early summer, it produces small white flowers with five rounded petals that look like tiny wild roses. The plant's most distinctive feature is its three-part leaves that turn gorgeous shades of red and orange in fall, earning it the nickname 'wineleaf.'

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery leaves divided into three leaflets, each ending in three distinct teeth. Feel waxy and tough between your fingers, staying green through most of the growing season before turning brilliant red-orange in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers about half an inch across with five rounded petals and a yellow center. Appear in loose clusters above the foliage in June and July, smelling faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, carpet-like mats that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall but spreading several feet wide. Stems are woody at the base and feel sturdy when gently pressed.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems develop thin, papery bark that peels in small strips. The woody base feels surprisingly solid for such a low plant and helps distinguish it from herbaceous look-alikes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny, dry fruits that cluster together where the flowers once bloomed. Each seed head feels rough and papery to the touch, persisting into late summer.

habitat: Three-toothed cinquefoil thrives in harsh, rocky environments throughout New England's mountains and exposed coastlines. Look for it on granite ledges, rocky summits, sandy shores, and thin soils where few other plants can survive. It's particularly common on mountain peaks and coastal bluffs where wind and weather create challenging growing conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, bright green leaves with the distinctive three-toothed tips becoming visible. The woody base begins showing signs of life with tiny leaf buds swelling.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in June and July with small white blooms covering the low mats. Leaves are at their thickest and most leathery, providing the best opportunity to feel their waxy texture.
seasonality.fall: The real showstopper season when leaves transform into brilliant reds, oranges, and purples, creating stunning carpets of color across rocky landscapes. This fall color display is often more reliable than flowers for identification.
seasonality.winter: Persistent woody stems and dried seed heads remain visible above snow, while some leaves may persist in protected spots. The plant's low, spreading structure becomes most apparent when other vegetation dies back.

funFact: Three-toothed cinquefoil is so tough it can survive being completely submerged under ice for months on mountain peaks, then bounce back to create some of New England's most spectacular fall color displays on seemingly barren rocky summits.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with wild strawberry, which also has three-leaflet leaves, but strawberry leaves are soft and thin while three-toothed cinquefoil's are thick and waxy. Remember: if the leaves feel like leather and end in exactly three teeth, you've found your cinquefoil.
contextualKnowledge: This plant has gone through several scientific name changes and was formerly classified as Potentilla tridentata, so you might see it listed under that name in older field guides. Despite being called a 'cinquefoil' (five-leaf), it's actually the only species in its genus and doesn't follow the typical five-leaflet pattern of true cinquefoils.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Sibbaldiopsis found in New England, three-toothed cinquefoil is unique among its immediate relatives. Within the broader rose family, it's distinguished from other low-growing members like wild strawberry by its woody stems and thick, waxy leaves, and from true cinquefoils (Potentilla species) by having three-part rather than five-part leaflets. Its combination of woody growth habit and three-toothed leaves makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
